reference.source: Primer on the Metabolic Bone Diseases and Disorders of Mineral Metabolism (ASBMR)
clinicalPearls: Caused by post-zygotic activating mutations in GNAS, producing a mosaic distribution so disease can be monostotic or polyostotic
Normal bone and marrow are replaced by expansile fibro-osseous tissue, giving the classic radiographic ground-glass appearance
When combined with cafe-au-lait macules (often with irregular coast-of-Maine borders) and endocrine hyperfunction such as precocious puberty, the picture is McCune-Albright syndrome
Associated endocrinopathies include precocious puberty, thyrotoxicosis, growth-hormone excess, and Cushing syndrome, all reflecting autonomous glandular activation
Craniofacial lesions may cause facial asymmetry, dental problems, and, if foramina are narrowed, visual or hearing compromise
The bone lesions can oversecrete FGF23, producing renal phosphate wasting and hypophosphataemic osteomalacia that aggravates deformity and fracture risk
Management is largely supportive with orthopaedic correction of deformity and fracture, treatment of associated endocrinopathy, and bisphosphonates considered for bone pain
reference.pathophysiology: Fibrous dysplasia arises from somatic gain-of-function mutations in the GNAS gene encoding the alpha subunit of the stimulatory G protein, leading to constitutive activation of adenylate cyclase and elevated cyclic AMP in affected cells. Because the mutation occurs after fertilisation, the resulting mosaicism explains the variable and patchy distribution of disease. In bone, the mutation impairs osteoblast differentiation so that normal bone marrow is replaced by disorganised fibrous stroma with immature woven bone. The same signalling defect in endocrine tissue drives autonomous hormone secretion, and lesional cells can produce excess FGF23, causing renal phosphate wasting.
additionalDifferentials: Ossifying fibroma and other fibro-osseous jaw lesions
Enchondroma or other benign bone tumour
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiographs showing ground-glass lucency, cortical thinning, and deformity such as the shepherd's-crook femur
Whole-body bone scintigraphy to map polyostotic disease
Serum alkaline phosphatase and bone turnover markers
Serum phosphate and FGF23 assessment for renal phosphate wasting
Endocrine screening for precocious puberty, thyroid, growth-hormone, and cortisol excess
Targeted imaging or biopsy where malignant change is suspected
redFlags: New or worsening bone pain, rapid swelling, or a soft-tissue mass suggesting malignant transformation
Cranial lesions causing visual loss, proptosis, or hearing deterioration
Signs of a functioning endocrine tumour such as thyrotoxic crisis or Cushingoid features
reference.prognosis: Monostotic disease is often mild and stable, whereas extensive polyostotic disease and McCune-Albright syndrome can cause progressive deformity, recurrent fractures, and endocrine morbidity; malignant transformation is rare but serious.
pitfalls: Mistaking a ground-glass lesion for a more aggressive tumour and performing unnecessary radical surgery
Overlooking associated endocrinopathy in a child presenting with bone disease and cafe-au-lait spots
Missing FGF23-mediated hypophosphataemia that worsens bone weakness
Attributing all new pain to benign disease and failing to investigate possible sarcomatous change
references: Primer on the Metabolic Bone Diseases and Disorders of Mineral Metabolism (ASBMR)
International consensus guidelines on fibrous dysplasia / McCune-Albright syndrome
management: Bisphosphonates to reduce bone pain from metabolically active lesions
Correction of FGF23-driven hypophosphataemic osteomalacia with oral phosphate and an active vitamin D metabolite such as calcitriol
Orthopaedic surgery for fracture fixation and correction of deformity such as the shepherd's-crook femur, with internal fixation of load-bearing lesions

Treatment of associated endocrinopathies in McCune-Albright syndrome: aromatase inhibitors or tamoxifen for precocious puberty, antithyroid therapy for thyrotoxicosis, and agents targeting growth-hormone or cortisol excess
Regular monitoring of bone turnover markers, serum phosphate and lesion progression, with surveillance for rare malignant transformation
Craniofacial surveillance for optic-nerve or auditory canal compromise, with decompression reserved for progressive deficit
Multidisciplinary care spanning metabolic bone, endocrinology, orthopaedics and craniofacial specialists
